Hands-On Exercise 9-2: Visual Correlation Analysis

Published

June 18, 2025

Modified

June 20, 2025

9-2: 1 Overview

Correlation coefficient is a popular statistic used to measure the type and strength of the relationship between two variables. The values of a correlation coefficient ranges between -1.0 and 1.0. A correlation coefficient of 1 shows a perfect linear relationship between the two variables, while -1.0 shows a perfect inverse relationship between the two variables. A correlation coefficient of 0.0 shows no linear relationship between the two variables.

When multivariate data are used, the correlation coefficients of the pair comparisons are displayed in a table form known as correlation matrix or scatterplot matrix.

There are three broad reasons for computing a correlation matrix.

  • To reveal the relationship between high-dimensional variables pair-wisely
  • To input into other analyses. For example, people commonly use correlation matrices as inputs for exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation models, and linear regression when excluding missing values pairwise.
  • As a diagnostic tool when checking other analyses. For example, a linear regression with a high amount of correlations suggests that the linear regression’s estimate will be unreliable.

When the data is large, both in terms of the number of observations and the number of variables, Corrgram tend to be used to visually explore and analyse the structure and the patterns of relations among variables.

Corrgram is designed based on two main schemes:

  • Rendering the value of a correlation to depict its sign and magnitude
  • Reordering the variables in a correlation matrix so that “similar” variables are positioned adjacently, facilitating perception

This exercise will cover how to plot data visualisation for visualising correlation matrix with R. It consists of three main sections.:

  1. How to create correlation matrix using [pairs()](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/graphics/versions/3.6.0/topics/pairs of R Graphics
  2. How to plot a corrgram using corrplot package of R
  3. How to create an interactive correlation matrix using plotly R.

9-2: 2 Install and Launch R Packages

The code below installs and launches corrplot, ggpubr, plotly and tidyverse in R studio.

Show Code 
pacman::p_load(corrplot, ggstatsplot, tidyverse, patchwork)

9-2: 3 Import data

The Wine Quality Data Set of UCI Machine Learning Repository will be used for this exercise. The data set consists of 13 variables and 6497 observations. For the purpose of this exercise, the red and white wine data have been combined into one data file called wine_quality and is in csv file format.

Show Code 
wine <- read_csv("data/wine_quality.csv")
Note

Besides type, the rest of the variables are in numerical and continuous data type.

Warning

Notes says quality is in character type?

9-2: 4 Build Correlation Matrix: pairs() method

We will use pairs function of R Graphics to create a scatterplot matrix. There are many other ways to do so, too. See pairs function.

There are more than one way to build scatterplot matrix with R. In this section, a scatterplot matrix will be created using the pairs function of R Graphics. Please refer to the linked syntax description of the pairs function.

9-2: 4.1 Build a Basic Correlation Matrix

Figure below shows the scatterplot matrix of Wine Quality Data in a 11 by 11 matrix.

The required input of pairs() can be a matrix or data frame. The code chunk used to create the scatterplot matrix is relatively simple. It uses the default pairs function.

Columns 1 to 11 of wine dataframe are used to build the first scatterplot matrix. The variables are: fixed acidity, volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlorides, free sulfur dioxide, total sulfur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates and alcohol.

Columns 2 to 12 of wine dataframe are used to build the second scatterplot matrix. The variables are: volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlorides, free sulfur dioxide, total sulfur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates, alcohol and quality.

  • Columns 1-11
  • Columns 2-12
Show Code 
pairs(wine[,1:11],
      main = "Correlation Matrix")
Show Code 
pairs(wine[,2:12],
      main = "Correlation Matrix")

Adding a function to wrap the column labels so that they can be viewed within the correlation matrix boxes.

Show Code 
# Function to wrap text into multiple lines
wrap_text <- function(x, width = 10) {
  sapply(x, function(s) {
    paste(strwrap(s, width = width), collapse = "\n")
  })
}

# Apply to column names
colnames(wine) <- wrap_text(colnames(wine))

pairs(wine[,1:11],
      cex.labels = 0.5)

9-2: 4.2 Draw the Lower Corner Only

The pairs function of R Graphics provided many customisation arguments. For example, it is a common practice to show either the upper half or lower half of the correlation matrix instead of both. This is because a correlation matrix is symmetric.

To show only the lower half of the correlation matrix, the upper.panel argument will be used as shown in the code chunk below.

Similarly, the upper half of the correlation matrix can be displayed by using the lower.panel arguement.

  • Lower Half
  • Upper Half
Show Code 
pairs(wine[,2:12], upper.panel = NULL,
      cex.labels = 0.5)
Show Code 
par(bg = "#f1f4f5")
pairs(wine[,2:12], lower.panel = NULL,
      cex.labels = 0.5)

9-2: 4.3 Include Correlation Coefficients

To show the correlation coefficient of each pair of variables inside a scatter plot, panel.cor function can be used. This will also show higher correlations in a larger font.

  • Default
  • Improved
Show Code 
panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
usr <- par("usr")
on.exit(par(usr))
par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

pairs(wine[,2:12], 
      upper.panel = panel.cor,
      cex.labels = 0.5)
Warning

on.exit(par(usr)) is giving an code warning

Show Code 
panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
usr <- par("usr")
on.exit(par(usr = usr))
par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

pairs(wine[,2:12], 
      upper.panel = panel.cor,
      cex.labels = 0.5)
Tip

using on.exit(par(usr = usr)) fixes the code warning

9-2: 5 Visualise Correlation Matrix: ggcormat()

One of the major limitation of the correlation matrix is that the scatter plots can appear to be very cluttered when the number of observations is relatively large (i.e. more than 500 observations). To over come this problem, Corrgram data visualisation technique suggested by D. J. Murdoch and E. D. Chow (1996) and Friendly, M (2002) will be applied.

These are three R packages that provides function to plot a corrgram:

  • corrgram
  • ellipse
  • corrplot

On top that, some R package like ggstatsplot package also provides functions for building corrgram.

This section will cover using ggcorrmat() of ggstatsplot package to visualise a correlation matrix.

9-2: 5.1 The Basic Plot

On of the advantage of using ggcorrmat() over many other methods to visualise a correlation matrix is its ability to provide a comprehensive and professional statistical report as shown in the figure below.

  • Default
  • Improved
Show Code 
ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11)
Show Code 
ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  ggplot.component = list(
    theme(text = element_text(size = 12),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12)
          )
  )
)
  • Default
  • Improved
Show Code 
ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  title    = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four pairs are no significant at p < 0.05"
)
Show Code 
ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  title    = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four pairs are no significant at p < 0.05",
  ggplot.component = list(
    theme(text = element_text(size = 12),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12)
          )
  )
)
Things to learn from the code
  • cor.vars argument is used to compute the correlation matrix needed to build the corrgram.
  • ggcorrplot.args argument provide additional (mostly aesthetic) arguments that will be passed to ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot function. The list should avoid any of the following arguments since they are already internally being used: corr, method, p.mat, sig.level, ggtheme, colors, lab, pch, legend.title, digits.

The sample sub-code chunk below can be used to control specific component of the plot such as the font size of the x-axis, y-axis, and the statistical report.

ggplot.component = list(
  theme(text = element_text(size = 5),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8))
)

9-2: 6 Build Multiple Plots

Since ggstasplot is an extension of ggplot2, it also supports faceting. However, the feature is not available in ggcorrmat() but in *grouped_ggcorrmat()* of ggstatsplot.

  • Default
  • Improved
Show the code 
grouped_ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  grouping.var = type,
  type = "robust",
  p.adjust.method = "holm",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2),
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  annotation.args = list(
    tag_levels = "a",
    title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
    subtitle = "The measures are: alcohol, sulphates, fixed acidity, citric acid, chlorides, residual sugar, density, free sulfur dioxide and volatile acidity",
    caption = "Dataset: UCI Machine Learning Repository"
  )
)
Show Code 
# fig-height: 8
# fig-width: 16
grouped_ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  grouping.var = type,
  type = "robust",
  p.adjust.method = "holm",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2),
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  annotation.args = list(
    tag_levels = "a",
    title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
    subtitle = "The measures are: alcohol, sulphates, fixed acidity, citric acid, chlorides, residual sugar, density, free sulfur dioxide and volatile acidity",
    caption = "Dataset: UCI Machine Learning Repository"
  ),
  ggplot.component = list(
    theme(text = element_text(size = 12),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12)
          )
  )
)
Things to learn from the code
  • fig-height and fig-width are used to expand the plotting area
  • To build a facet plot, the only argument needed is grouping.var
  • Behind group_ggcorrmat(), patchwork package is used to create the multiplot. plotgrid.args argument provides a list of additional arguments passed to patchwork::wrap_plots. This excludes guides argument which is already specified separately earlier.
  • Likewise, annotation.args argument is calling the plot annotation arguments of patchwork package.

9-2: 7 Visualise Correlation Matrix Using corrplot Package

In section we will focus on corrplot and more information can be found in the link An Introduction to corrplot Package to gain a better understanding of the corrplot package.

9-2: 7.1 Get Started with corrplot

The correlation matrix of wine data frame needs to be computed before plotting a corrgram using corrplot(). In the code chunk below, cor() of R Stats is used to compute the correlation matrix of wine data frame.

Show Code 
wine.cor <- cor(wine[,1:11])

Next, corrplot() is used to plot the corrgram by using all the default settingsas shown in the code chunk below.

Show Code 
corrplot(wine.cor)
Note
  • Default visual object: Circle
  • Default layout: Symmetric matrix
  • Default colour scheme: Diverging blue-red
    • Blue colours are used to represent pair variables with positive correlation coefficients and red colours are used to represent pair variables with negative correlation coefficients
  • The intensity of the colour or also know as saturation is used to represent the strength of the correlation coefficient
    • Darker colours indicates a relatively stronger linear relationship between the paired variables
    • On the other hand, lighter colours indicates relatively weaker linear relationship

9-2: 7.2 Work with Visual Geometrics

In the corrplot package, there are seven visual geometrics (parameter method) that can be used to encode the attribute values.

They are: circle, square, ellipse, number, shade, colour and pie.

The default is circle as shown in the previous section, the default visual geometric of the corrplot matrix is circle. However, this default setting can be changed by using the method argument as shown in the code chunk below.

  • Circle
  • Square
  • Ellipse
  • Number
  • Shade
  • Color
  • Pie
Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "circle")
Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "square")
Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse")
Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "number")
Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "shade")
Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "color")
Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "pie")

9-2: 7.3 Work with Layout

corrplor() supports three layout types, namely: full, upper or lower.

The default is full which display the full matrix. The default setting can be changed by using the type argument of corrplot().

Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower")

The default layout of the corrgram can be further customised. For example, arguments diag and tl.col can be used to turn off the diagonal cells and to change the axis text label colour to black respectively as shown in the code chunk and figure below.

Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black")

Further layout customisation can be done using l.pos, tl.cex, tl.offset, cl.pos, cl.cex and cl.offset.

Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower",
         
         # Text label (variable names) adjustments
         tl.pos = "ld",     # Position: 'l' (left), 'd' (diagonal), or 'ld' (both)
         tl.cex = 0.8,      # Text label size (default=1)
         tl.offset = 0.5,   # Space between text and plot (default=0.4)
         tl.srt = 45,       # Text rotation angle (optional)
        
         # Color legend adjustments
         cl.pos = "r",      # Position: 'r' (right), 'b' (bottom), or 'n' (none)
         cl.cex = 0.8,      # Color legend text size (default=0.8)
         cl.offset = 0.75,  # Space between legend and plot (default=0.5)
)

9-2: 7.4 Work with mixed layout

With corrplot package, it is possible to design corrgram with mixed visual matrix of one half and numerical matrix on the other half. In order to create a coorgram with mixed layout, the corrplot.mixed(), a wrapped function for mixed visualisation style will be used.

Show the code 
corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")
Things to learn from the code
  • The argument lower and upper are used to define the visualisation method used
  • Ellipse is used to map the lower half of the corrgram and numerical matrix (i.e. number) is used to map the upper half of the corrgram
  • The argument tl.pos, on the other, is used to specify the placement of the axis label
  • The diag argument is used to specify the glyph on the principal diagonal of the corrgram

9-2: 7.5 Combine corrgram with the Significance Test

In statistical analysis, it is also of interest to know which pair of variables have statistically significant correlation coefficients.

Figure below shows a corrgram combined with the significance test. The corrgram reveals that not all correlation pairs are statistically significant. For example, the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free surfur dioxide is statistically significant at significant level of 0.1 but not the pair between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid.

With the corrplot package, the cor.mtest() can be used to compute the p-values and confidence interval for each pair of variables.

Show Code 
wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level= .95)

Then the p.mat argument of corrplot function can be used as shown in the code chunk below.

Show Code 
corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)

9-2: 7.6 Reorder a corrgram

Matrix reorder is very important for mining the hidden structure and pattern in a corrgram. By default, the order of attributes of a corrgram is sorted according to the correlation matrix (i.e. “original”). The default setting can be over-written by using the order argument of corrplot().

Currently, corrplot package supports four sorting methods, they are:

  • “AOE” is for the angular order of the eigenvectors. See Michael Friendly (2002) in Section 8 Reference for details.
  • “FPC” for the first principal component order
  • “hclust” for hierarchical clustering order, and “hclust.method” for the agglomeration method to be used
    • “hclust.method” should be one of “ward”, “single”, “complete”, “average”, “mcquitty”, “median” or “centroid”
  • “alphabet” for alphabetical order.

“AOE”, “FPC”, “hclust”, “alphabet” and other algorithms can be found in seriation package.

Show the code 
corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               order="AOE",
               tl.col = "black")

9-2: 7.7 Reorder a Correlation Matrix using hclust

Using hclust allows corrplot() to draw rectangles around the corrgram based on the results of hierarchical clustering.

Show the code 
corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         order="hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)

9-2: 8 Reference

  • Michael Friendly (2002). “Corrgrams: Exploratory displays for correlation matrices”. The American Statistician, 56, 316–324
  • D.J. Murdoch, E.D. Chow (1996). “A graphical display of large correlation matrices”. The American Statistician, 50, 178–180

9-2: 8.1 R packages

  • ggcormat() of ggstatsplot package
  • ggscatmat and ggpairs of GGally.
  • corrplot. A graphical display of a correlation matrix or general matrix. It also contains some algorithms to do matrix reordering. In addition, corrplot is good at details, including choosing color, text labels, color labels, layout, etc.
  • corrgram calculates correlation of variables and displays the results graphically. Included panel functions can display points, shading, ellipses, and correlation values with confidence intervals.
